extracted.intended_audience: Employers, workplace safety professionals, supervisors, and heat safety coordinators responsible for complying with OSHA workplace standards
extracted.subtask_description: Complying with the proposed OSHA Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard (29 CFR 1910.148 and parallel sections) by developing and implementing required plans, controls, monitoring, training, and recordkeeping to prevent heat-related injuries and illnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and application — general applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided in this paragraph (a), this standard applies to all employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific exceptions (paragraph (a)(2)) and notes employers whose employees exclusively perform exempted activities are exempt from the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and application — specified exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: This standard does not apply to: (i) work activities with no reasonable expectation of exposure at/above the initial heat trigger; (ii) short duration employee exposures at/above the initial heat trigger of 15 minutes or less in any 60-minute period; (iii) organizations whose primary function is firefighting or certain emergency response activities already covered under listed standards; (iv) indoor work areas or vehicles where air-conditioning consistently keeps ambient temperature below 80 °F; (v) telework; and (vi) sedentary indoor work activities involving sitting, occasional standing/walking, and occasional lifting under 10 pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers whose employees exclusively perform activities in (i)-(vi) are exempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference — NIOSH 2016-106
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH Publication No. 2016-106, Criteria for a Recommended Standard: Occupational Exposure to Heat and Hot Environments, February 2016, is incorporated by reference for specified alert and exposure limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IBR approved for §1910.148(b); defines Recommended Alert Limit (RAL) and Recommended Exposure Limit (REL) used elsewhere in the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — acclimatization
rubrics_metrics.description: Acclimatization means the body's adaptation to work in the heat as a person is exposed to heat gradually over time, which reduces the strain caused by heat stress and enables a person to work with less chance of heat illness or injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — ambient temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambient temperature means the temperature of the air surrounding a body. It is also called 'air temperature' or 'dry bulb temperature.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — cooling personal protective equipment (PPE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooling personal protective equipment (PPE) means equipment worn to protect the user against heat injury or illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — heat index
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat index means the National Weather Service heat index, which combines ambient temperature and humidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — high heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: High heat trigger means a heat index of 90 °F or a wet bulb globe temperature equal to the NIOSH Recommended Exposure Limit (REL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial heat trigger means a heat index of 80 °F or a wet bulb globe temperature equal to the NIOSH Recommended Alert Limit (RAL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — indoor/indoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoor/indoors means an area under a ceiling or overhead covering that restricts airflow and has along its entire perimeter walls, doors, windows, dividers, or other physical barriers that restrict airflow, whether open or closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — outdoor/outdoors
rubrics_metrics.description: Outdoor/outdoors means an area that is not indoors. For purposes of this standard, vehicles operated outdoors are considered outdoor work areas unless exempted by paragraph (a)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — radiant heat
rubrics_metrics.description: Radiant heat means heat transferred by electromagnetic waves between surfaces. Sources include the sun, hot objects, hot liquids, hot surfaces, and fire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Shade means the blockage of direct sunlight, such that objects do not cast a shadow in the area of blocked sunlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — signs and symptoms of a heat emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs and symptoms of a heat emergency means physiological manifestations that require emergency response and includes loss of consciousness with excessive body temperature, which may include vertigo, nausea, headache, cerebral dysfunction, bizarre behavior, staggering, vomiting, convulsions, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — signs and symptoms of heat-related illness
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs and symptoms of heat-related illness means physiological manifestations including headache, nausea, weakness, dizziness, elevated body temperature, muscle cramps, and muscle pain or spasms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — vapor-impermeable clothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Vapor-impermeable clothing means full-body clothing that significantly inhibits or prevents sweat evaporation (examples: encapsulating suits, chemical resistant suits, other nonbreathable PPE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions — wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT) means a heat metric that takes into account ambient temperature, humidity, radiant heat, and air movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat injury and illness prevention plan (HIIPP) — creation and site-specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must develop and implement a work site heat injury and illness prevention plan (HIIPP) with site-specific information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plan must be tailored to the work site and include specific items listed in paragraph (c)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP — required contents
rubrics_metrics.description: The HIIPP must include: (i) a comprehensive list of types of work activities covered; (ii) all policies and procedures necessary to comply with the standard; and (iii) identification of the heat metric (heat index or WBGT) the employer will monitor to comply with monitoring requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If employees wear vapor-impermeable clothing, the HIIPP must include an evaluation and policies/procedures based on reputable sources and document the evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP — written plan threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: If the employer has more than 10 employees, the HIIPP must be written.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP — heat safety coordinator designation
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must designate one or more heat safety coordinators to implement and monitor the HIIPP and document their identity in any written HIIPP. Coordinators must have the authority to ensure compliance with all aspects of the HIIPP.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP — employee involvement and review
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must seek input and involvement of non-managerial employees and their representatives in developing and implementing the HIIPP, review and evaluate effectiveness whenever a qualifying heat-related illness/injury occurs and at least annually, and update the HIIPP as necessary with employee input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualifying incidents for review: death, days away from work, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: HIIPP — availability and language
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must make the HIIPP readily available at the work site to all employees performing work at the site, and the HIIPP must be available in a language each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying heat hazards — outdoor monitoring options
rubrics_metrics.description: For outdoor work, the employer must monitor heat conditions by either tracking local heat index forecasts provided by the National Weather Service or other reputable sources, or by measuring at/near the work area either heat index (or ambient temperature and humidity separately) or WBGT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying heat hazards — frequency of outdoor monitoring
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must monitor with sufficient frequency to determine with reasonable accuracy employees' exposure to heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying heat hazards — indoor monitoring and plans
rubrics_metrics.description: For indoor work, the employer must identify each work area where there is a reasonable expectation of exposure at/above the initial heat trigger, develop and implement a monitoring plan covering each identified area that measures heat index (or ambient temperature and humidity) or WBGT at/near the area, and update evaluations/plans whenever changes potentially increase indoor heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring plans must be included in the HIIPP; employers must seek input of non-managerial employees when evaluating and updating monitoring plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat metric selection determines triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: The heat metric the employer chooses to monitor determines the applicable initial and high heat triggers for the standard. If the employer does not identify a choice or monitor as required, the initial and high heat triggers will be the heat index values in the definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption from monitoring by assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer can assume a work area is at or above both the initial and high heat triggers instead of conducting on-site measurements or tracking forecasts; in such cases the employer must provide all control measures outlined for those triggers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger — timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must implement the controls described in paragraph (e) when employees are exposed to heat at or above the initial heat trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger — drinking water
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must provide access to potable drinking water that is (i) placed in locations readily accessible to the employee; (ii) suitably cool; and (iii) of sufficient quantity to provide access to 1 quart of drinking water per employee per hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements are in addition to sanitation standards and temporary labor camps standards; see Note 1 to paragraph (e)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger — outdoor break areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must provide one or more break area(s) for employees that accommodate the number on break, are readily accessible, and have at least one of: (i) artificial or natural shade open to the outside air (not shade from equipment), or (ii) air-conditioning if enclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger — indoor break areas
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must provide one or more break area(s) for employees that is air-conditioned or has increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification, can accommodate the number on break, and is readily accessible to the work areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the initial heat trigger — indoor work area controls
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must provide at each identified indoor work area one of: (i) increased air movement (fans or comparable natural ventilation) and de-humidification if appropriate; (ii) air-conditioned work area; or (iii) for radiant heat sources, other effective measures (shielding/barriers, isolating heat sources).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of fan use
rubrics_metrics.description: At ambient temperatures above 102 °F, if the employer provides fans to comply with indoor controls or break area requirements, the employer must evaluate humidity to determine if fan use is harmful, and discontinue fan use if it is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization — new employees protocol options
rubrics_metrics.description: For each new employee during their first week on the job, the employer must implement one of: (A) a plan that at minimum incorporates the measures in paragraph (f) whenever the heat index is at/above the initial trigger during the first week; or (B) gradual acclimatization restricting exposure to no more than 20% of a normal shift on day 1, 40% day 2, 60% day 3, and 80% day 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization — returning employees protocol options
rubrics_metrics.description: For employees away >14 days, during their first week back the employer must implement one of: (A) a plan that at minimum incorporates measures in paragraph (f) whenever the heat index is at/above the initial trigger; or (B) gradual acclimatization restricting exposure to no more than 50% of a normal shift on day 1, 60% day 2, and 80% day 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: requirements do not apply if employer demonstrates the employee consistently worked under same or similar conditions within prior 14 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks if needed at initial trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must allow and encourage employees to take paid rest breaks in the required break area if needed to prevent overheating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective two-way communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must maintain a means of effective, two-way communication with employees (e.g., voice or electronic means) and regularly communicate with employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling PPE maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the employer provides employees with cooling PPE, the employer must ensure the cooling properties of the PPE are maintained at all times during use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls required at or above the high heat trigger — timing
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to initial-trigger controls, the employer must implement the controls described in paragraph (f) when employees are exposed to heat at or above the high heat trigger.

rubrics_metrics.name: High trigger — rest breaks required
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must provide employees a minimum 15-minute paid rest break at least every two hours in the required break area, subject to: (i) a meal break may count as a rest break even if unpaid; (ii) donning/doffing PPE must not count towards total rest time; and (iii) walk time to/from break area not included in rest time.

rubrics_metrics.name: High trigger — observation for signs and symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must implement at least one observation method: (i) mandatory buddy system; or (ii) observation by supervisor or heat safety coordinator with no more than 20 employees observed per observer. For lone workers, maintain two-way communications and make contact at least every two hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: High trigger — Hazard Alert requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to the shift or upon determining the high heat trigger is met/exceeded, the employer must notify employees of: (i) importance of drinking plenty of water; (ii) employees' right to take rest breaks if needed and required rest breaks; (iii) how to seek help and procedures in a heat emergency; and (iv) for mobile worksites, location of break areas and drinking water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessively high heat areas signage
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer must place warning signs at indoor work areas with ambient temperatures that regularly exceed 120 °F. Signs must be legible, visible, and understandable to employees entering the work areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat emergency response plan — required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: As part of the HIIPP, the employer must develop and implement a heat emergency response plan including: (i) emergency phone numbers; (ii) how employees can contact a supervisor and EMS; (iii) designated individual(s) to invoke heat emergency procedures; (iv) how to transport employees to reach EMS; (v) clear and precise directions to the work site (address) for dispatchers; and (vi) procedures for responding to employees with signs/symptoms, including suspected heat stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat emergency response — employer actions for non-emergency heat illness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee is experiencing signs and symptoms of heat-related illness, the employer must: (i) relieve them from duty; (ii) monitor them; (iii) ensure they are not left alone; (iv) offer on-site first aid or medical services before ending monitoring; and (v) provide means to reduce body temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat emergency response — employer actions for heat emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: If an employee is experiencing signs and symptoms of a heat emergency, the employer must: (i) take immediate actions to reduce the employee's body temperature before EMS arrive; (ii) contact EMS immediately; and (iii) perform the non-emergency measures (relieve, monitor, not leave alone, offer first aid) in (g)(2)(i)-(iv).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — initial training topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to any work at/above the initial heat trigger, the employer must ensure each employee receives training and understands: (i) heat stress hazards; (ii) heat-related injuries/illnesses; (iii) risk factors including exertion, clothing/PPE, lack of acclimatization, and personal risk factors; (iv) signs/symptoms requiring immediate emergency action; (v) importance of removing PPE that impairs cooling during rest breaks; (vi) importance of taking paid rest breaks; (vii) importance of drinking water; (viii) location of break areas; (ix) location of employer-provided water; (x) importance of reporting signs/symptoms in self/others; (xi) all HIIPP policies/procedures applicable to duties; (xii) identity of heat safety coordinator(s); (xiii) requirements of this standard; (xiv) how to access the HIIPP; (xv) employees' rights and anti-discrimination protections for exercising those rights; and (xvi) procedures for excessively high heat areas if applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — supervisor and heat safety coordinator training
rubrics_metrics.description: Supervisors responsible for employees performing work at/above the initial trigger and heat safety coordinators must be trained on the topics in paragraph (h)(1) and additionally: (i) policies/procedures developed to comply with the standard, including monitoring policies; and (ii) procedures the supervisor or coordinator must follow if an employee exhibits signs/symptoms of heat-related illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — annual refresher and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Each employee must receive annual training on topics in (h)(1); supervisors and heat safety coordinators must receive annual training on topics in (h)(2). For outdoor employees, annual refresher training must be conducted before or at the start of heat season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — supplemental training triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide prompt additional training whenever: (i) changes occur that affect heat exposure (e.g., new job tasks); (ii) employer changes applicable policies/procedures; (iii) there is indication an employee hasn't retained necessary understanding; or (iv) a qualifying heat-related injury/illness occurs at the work site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training — presentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Training must be provided in a language and at a literacy level each employee, supervisor, and heat safety coordinator understands, and employers must provide opportunity for questions and answers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping — indoor on-site measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the employer conducts on-site measurements at indoor work areas pursuant to paragraph (d)(3)(ii), they must have written or electronic records of those indoor work area measurements and retain those records for 6 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost — employer responsibility to bear costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The implementation of all requirements of this standard must be at no cost to employees, including paying employees their normal rate of pay when compliance requires employee time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective dates — implementation timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective date: this standard is effective [60 days after date of publication of the final rule in the Federal Register]. Compliance date: Employers must comply with all requirements by [150 days after date of publication of the final rule in the Federal Register].

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each provision within this standard is separate and severable. If any provision is held invalid or unenforceable on its face or as applied, that provision shall be construed to give maximum effect permitted by law, or severed if utterly invalid, without affecting remainder of the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel applicability across OSHA parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements set forth at 29 CFR 1910.148 are made applicable identically to other OSHA parts: shipyard employment (1915.95), marine terminals (1917.32), and longshoring operations (1918.148).
